claims.assertion: The trip is a RydeTAXI metered trip (total charged $42.52 metered), so RydeTAXI metered fare rules govern the disputed distance rather than a fixed quote.

The rider overstated the fare by conflating the app estimate with the meter: the complaint says 'about 15 km' and 'almost 20 km', but the recorded figures are 15.5 km optimal vs 20.1 km actual, and the fare charged is $42.52.

Only one off-route segment is alleged on the record: 12:46–13:07, 9.70 km driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km — so any metered-distance adjustment must be confined to that single segment under RD-1/RD-2.

The driver's GPS chose the fastest route: at the time of the deviation the main optimal expressway was flowing at 60–69 km/h (band 7) while Paya Lebar Road, the corridor he stayed on, was in band 3 (20–29 km/h), and Ryde expressly permits a driver to take the fastest or most efficient GPS route.

No traffic incident (accident, roadwork, breakdown, road block, heavy traffic) is recorded near the route during the trip window and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, so the reroute cannot be justified as an incident-driven detour and the RD-4(a) incident defence is not available to my client.
Speed-band evidence alone (band 3 on Paya Lebar Road, band 7 on the expressways) is at most corroborative under RD-4(b) and cannot by itself exempt the 4.08 km segment.

There is no in-app chat log at all, so there is no rider consent on record before the segment started and no route-change message from the driver either; RP-3(b) therefore does not exempt the segment, though the absence of a chat record also means there was no in-app route discussion between the parties.

The driver's explanation ('I followed my GPS, it took me off at Paya Lebar. Nothing wrong with the fare') is a post-trip written statement, not a recorded consent message by the rider, and it is contradicted by the GPS off-route fact F3, so it cannot defeat the system record.

Because the off-route segment is unexempted, the refusal to address the excess is not warranted, and the correct voluntary adjustment is confined to the excess distance actually billed at the trip's per-km rate: $6.50 for the 4.6 km excess (4.6 km × $1.41/km), which is the ceiling on any return on this record.

No ERP or toll item appears in the charged breakdown (base $3.90, distance $28.31, time $8.84, waiting $0.00, platform $1.47), so no ERP/toll component can be refunded on top of the distance adjustment.

The driver has 640 trips in the last 90 days, a 4.8 rating and a single dispute with zero upheld, so this is not the 'repeated' violation pattern that RD-6's flag_account add-on addresses and no account flag is warranted against my client.
The fare charged reflects the full metered distance of 20.1 km with no unlisted add-on, so on the fare schedule itself nothing above the RD-2 distance adjustment is refundable.

weaknesses: The core weakness is the unexempted deviation itself: F3 shows 9.70 km driven where the optimal route covers 5.62 km, adding 4.08 km and up to 1720 m from the optimal route, and RD-1 sets no percentage or kilometre threshold, so the deviation is a breach of the shortest-and-most-direct-route duty on its face.

F4 (excess billed $6.50 for 4.6 km × $1.41/km) and F6 (total $42.52 on a 20.1 km metered distance) are the rider's arithmetic and will support a refund_partial of roughly $6.50 unless the judge prefers to compute strictly per unexempted segment (4.08 km × $1.41/km ≈ $5.75); I cannot argue the excess away.

F8 (driver statement) and F12/F13 (no incident, fair weather, 0.0 mm rain) remove the RD-4 defences; F10/F11 speed bands are band 7 and band 3, not band 1/2, and RD-4(b) only corroborates and never exempts alone.

F7 shows there are no chat messages, so there is no rider consent admissible under RD-5 — a driver statement that the rider agreed verbally (G11) would not have saved the segment, and we have none recorded.
F1 (+4.6 km, +30%) and F2 (+12.2 min over a 22 min estimate) are the headline figures the rider will quote to characterise the trip as a significant unexplained detour.
